meta.title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

lit.text:
The retrieved list is thin and mostly off-topic, so it says little directly about the hypotheses on source cues (tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge, conspiracy belief) and information type in sharing and plausibility. The closest items are general. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) discuss how misinformation spreads and influences people, and Roozenbeek et al. (2020) report predictors of belief in COVID-19 misinformation across countries, including links to health behaviours. Neither tests how sharer attributes shape sharing or plausibility, so neither bears on the AMCE estimates for H1-H14 or the weighted robustness checks R1-R12. Van Bavel et al. (2020) is a broad pandemic-response review with no abstract available. Three retrieved works are unrelated to the hypotheses: Dwivedi et al. (2019) on AI, Jenkins and Purushotma (2006) on media education, and Kniffin et al. (2020) on workplaces. The EMNLP 2021 proceedings entry (2021) is also unrelated. The works tagged as method concern attitudes toward the unvaccinated (Bor et al., 2022), election-lie acceptance (Arceneaux & Truex, 2022), and a vaccine-hesitancy survey with embedded conjoint experiments (Stamm et al., 2022). Only the last is a design precedent, as another conjoint on a health topic, and its abstract snippet reports no findings relevant here.

The retrieved works do not clearly disagree with each other or with the study's expectations, because none reports findings on the specific source-cue effects. The one tension is loose. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) frame misinformation as a broad societal problem, while Roozenbeek et al. (2020) locate susceptibility in individual and country-level predictors. Neither speaks to whether sharing depends on who shares, or to sharing without believing (X4). The study's conjoint design, which randomizes source attributes and measures both sharing and plausibility, can speak to that question directly, but the retrieved literature offers no benchmark against which to compare the estimates.

takeaways: In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.

Among measured sharer attributes, close ties were associated with 3.0 points more sharing (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust with 5.7 points more (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.
sections.abstract: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer relative to low trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.
sections.design_notes: Respondents were a YouGov sample of US adults. Of 12,000 raw profile ratings, the models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility. Each profile attributed a headline to one of the respondent's real contacts. Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact were randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are measured attributes of those contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes, not causal effects. True/neutral headlines are the reference level for information type (3,822 misinformation and 3,915 fact-check profiles in the sharing model). Standard errors are clustered by respondent, and tests are two-sided.

results.H1: Information type had large effects on sharing. Misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Chosen shares were 60.3% for true/neutral, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. These are causal contrasts, because headline type was randomized.
results.H2: Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p = 0.003). This is a descriptive contrast on a measured attribute.
results.H3: Continental US origin was 0.2 points above foreign origin (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.H4: A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p = 0.034), a small difference close to the threshold. Conservative sharers were not distinguishable from liberal ones (−0.7 points, 95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]).
results.H5: High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing than low trust (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p < 0.001). Mid trust was 3.6 points higher, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]).
results.H6: Neither mid nor high sharer knowledge was distinguishable from low. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]); mid was about zero.
results.H7: A sharer with high belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from one with low belief on sharing (−0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p = 0.87).
results.H8: Misinformation was rated 18.6 points less plausible than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 12.4 points less plausible (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p < 0.001). The pattern closely mirrors sharing.
results.H9: Close ties were associated with 2.8 points higher plausibility than distant ties (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p = 0.008), a modest contrast on a measured attribute.
results.H10: Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.3 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.4]).
results.H11: Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal ones (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p = 0.026), a small contrast near the threshold. Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.H12: Neither mid nor high trust was distinguishable from low for plausibility. High trust was 2.5 points higher (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]).
results.H13: Sharer knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]); mid was about zero.
results.H14: Sharer belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (0.0 points, 95% CI [−1.8, 1.8]).
results.RW: Re-weighting each source attribute by the inverse of its assignment probability left the picture largely unchanged. Close ties were still associated with 3.0 points more sharing and 2.7 points higher plausibility, and high trust with 6.7 points more sharing (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The weighted moderate-sharer contrast on sharing was −1.7 points (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0]) and is not significant at 0.05 (p = 0.056); on plausibility it stayed at −2.1 points. High trust on plausibility remained not distinguishable from zero. The other estimates were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S1: Age moderated the response to information type. Respondents in the highest age tertile shared misinformation 6.1 points less than the lowest tertile (p < 0.001). Differences for the other levels were not distinguishable from zero. These are descriptive subgroup contrasts.
results.S2: Respondent ideology mattered for a few levels. More conservative respondents shared true/neutral headlines 5.6 points less (p = 0.002), shared less from continental US sharers (−1.6 points, p = 0.005), and shared less from liberal sharers (−4.8 points, p = 0.017). Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S3: Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with the least (p < 0.001) and true/neutral headlines 5.5 points less (p < 0.001). They also shared less from high-trust sharers (−2.3 points, p < 0.001) and continental US sharers (−1.7 points, p = 0.002).
results.S4: Respondents with higher media trust shared misinformation 4.8 points more than those with low media trust (p = 0.003). They also shared less from high-knowledge sharers (−2.4 points, p = 0.028) and more from low-conspiracy sharers (+3.5 points, p = 0.032). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S5: Spanish-language respondents shared misinformation 3.6 points more than English-language ones (p = 0.010). They also shared more from low-trust sharers (+7.9 points, p = 0.022; cells of only 257 Spanish and 571 English profiles) and low-knowledge sharers (+3.2 points, p = 0.038). Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero, and with many comparisons some of these may be chance.
results.S6: Older respondents rated misinformation 4.0 points less plausible than younger ones (p = 0.013), and liberal sharers 3.7 points more plausible (p = 0.020). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S7: More conservative respondents rated true/neutral headlines 4.9 points less plausible (p = 0.006) and continental-US-attributed profiles 1.5 points less plausible (p = 0.009). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S8: Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims rated misinformation 6.8 points more plausible (p < 0.001) and true/neutral headlines 6.9 points less plausible (p < 0.001). They also gave lower plausibility to high-trust sharers (−2.4 points, p < 0.001) and high-knowledge sharers (−3.6 points, p = 0.002).
results.S9: Respondents with higher media trust rated misinformation 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-conspiracy sharers 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.009). They rated high-knowledge sharers 2.6 points less plausible (p = 0.019).
results.S10: Spanish-language respondents rated misinformation 3.7 points more plausible than English-language ones (p = 0.008). They also rated low-trust sharers 9.0 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-knowledge sharers 3.6 points more plausible (p = 0.016). These are subgroup contrasts among many tests.
results.X1: This is a post hoc analysis. Each extra point of trust in the sharer (on the 1–5 scale) was associated with 1.4 points more sharing (p < 0.001, two-sided).
results.X2: This is a post hoc analysis. Each extra point of trust was associated with 1.3 points higher plausibility (p < 0.001, two-sided).
results.X3: This is a post hoc analysis. The close-tie premium on sharing was 2.9 points (p = 0.006, two-sided), consistent with the registered estimate.
results.X4: Post hoc. Among profiles chosen for sharing, misinformation was 5.5 points more likely than true/neutral to be one the respondent judged less plausible than the other post (95% CI [3.0, 8.1], p < 0.001). Fact-checks were 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 4.0]).
results.X5: Post hoc. Sharing was 4.4 points higher when respondent and sharer leaned the same way than when they leaned opposite (95% CI [0.9, 7.9], p = 0.015). Pairs involving a moderate were not distinguishable from opposite leans (0.8 points).
results.X6: Post hoc. Among misinformation profiles, a higher network mean perceived belief in disputed claims was associated with more sharing (coefficient 0.110, p = 0.026, n = 3,196). This is a modest association, near the threshold.
results.X7: Post hoc. Among partisan respondents, congenial slanted headlines were shared 2.5 points more than uncongenial ones, not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.18, n = 3,016).
results.X8: Post hoc. The slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero overall (0.005, p = 0.71).
results.X9: Post hoc. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero overall (−0.005, p = 0.72).
results.X10: Post hoc and thin (n = 266). The anti-vaccine misinformation headline was rated 16.5 points more plausible when the sharer was seen as believing the DNA claim (p = 0.013). Treat with caution.
results.X11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 1.9 points per trust point across headlines (p = 0.013), a small association.
results.X12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing misinformation was 3.5 points (p = 0.040), near the threshold.
results.X13: Post hoc. Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero in the pooled slope (0.002, p = 0.78), matching H3.
results.XS1: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing was 1.7 points for fact-checks, 1.9 for misinformation and 0.6 for true/neutral headlines. The differences between slopes were not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS2: Post hoc. The trust slope on plausibility was about 1.8 points for fact-checks and 2.1 for misinformation, and about zero for true/neutral headlines. Differences between slopes were not clearly distinguishable.
results.XS3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium was 4.7 points for fact-checks, 3.5 for misinformation and 0.9 for true/neutral headlines. The gap between true/neutral and fact-checks was borderline (p = 0.050).
results.XS5: Post hoc. The congruent-versus-opposite sharing gap was between 3.8 and 5.6 points within each information type, with intervals including zero. The differences between types were not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS7: Post hoc. Congenial misinformation was shared 5.4 points more than uncongenial misinformation (p = 0.012), but there was no such gap for fact-checks (−0.2 points). The difference between the two was 5.6 points (p = 0.007).
results.XS8: Post hoc. For misinformation, sharing rose with the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (slope 0.086, p = 0.002), while slopes for fact-checks and true/neutral headlines were not distinguishable from zero. The difference from fact-checks was 0.131 (p = 0.001).
results.XS9: Post hoc. Plausibility of misinformation rose with the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief (slope 0.095, p < 0.001), but fell slightly for true/neutral headlines (−0.055, p = 0.046). The difference from fact-checks was 0.146 for misinformation (p < 0.001).
results.XS11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 2.5 points for health and 1.9 for political headlines. The difference was not distinguishable from zero, and the health group was small (n = 550).
results.XS12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on misinformation was 0.7 points for health and 3.9 for political headlines. The difference was not distinguishable from zero, and the health group was small.
results.XS13a: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was near zero in both English (0.004) and Spanish (0.000), and the difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS13b: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 1.3 points among foreign-born and −0.8 points among US-born respondents. Neither was distinguishable from zero, nor was the difference.

sections.limitations: Many tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so the smaller effects (moderate sharer, close tie on plausibility, several subgroup contrasts) may be chance findings. Only headline type was randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so those AMCEs bundle correlated attributes and are not causal. Non-significant results are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Health-topic and other subgroups are small. The exploratory X and XS analyses were specified after seeing the data and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

extensions.title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
extensions.why: Fixes the design cause: randomizing attributes in vignettes turns the descriptive close-tie and high-trust contrasts into causal estimates and removes bundling with the real contact.

power_target.basis: H2 close tie 0.030 vs MDE 0.0258; H5 high trust 0.057 vs MDE 0.051

extensions.rationale: In the source study close ties (+3.0 points, CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust (+5.7 points, CI [2.3, 9.1]) were associated with more sharing, but these attributes were respondents' ratings of real contacts and so bundle correlated traits. Randomizing tie and trust in a forwarded-post vignette tests whether they cause sharing of false headlines (misinformation was shared 18.2 points less than true headlines).
extensions.contribution: Turns descriptive tie-strength and trust contrasts into causal estimates, using a behavioural share outcome and a real-contact benchmark.
extensions.hypothesis: H1: a randomized close tie raises the probability of sharing by about 0.03. H2: randomized high trust raises it by about 0.05. Both effects hold for false headlines.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share of the forwarded post to the mock feed (binary).
extensions.comparison: Close vs distant tie and high vs low trust, within headline type. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. Headline type is a between-subject factor.
unresolved: The platform's randomization of tie and trust within each arm, the mock feed implementation, compensation and IRB number must be supplied by the research team.

extensions.title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
extensions.why: Fixes the missing_moderator cause: it pre-selects the moderator from S3 and S8 and tests it with enough power instead of relying on a tertile contrast.

power_target.basis: S3 misinformation difference 0.056 (SE 0.017); interaction MDE is larger than main-effect MDE 0.031

extensions.rationale: The source found misinformation shared 18.2 points less than true/neutral content (95% CI [-20.4,-16.0]), but respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more (p<0.001), a tertile contrast that was underpowered and US-English only. This design pre-selects belief in disputed claims as the moderator, stratifies on it and on survey language (English/Spanish), and tests one registered interaction.
extensions.contribution: Tests whether the misinformation sharing penalty shrinks among high-belief respondents and whether it generalizes to Spanish-language samples.
extensions.hypothesis: The gap in sharing between misinformation and true/neutral headlines is smaller among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims than in the bottom tertile (a positive infotype-by-moderator interaction). The penalty is present in both languages.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share: chosen/likely to share the headline (infotype x belief tertile interaction).
extensions.comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, interacted with belief tertile (top vs bottom), with respondent-clustered SEs; language is a secondary stratum.
unresolved: Actual headline images and Spanish translations must be supplied by the research team.
IRB number, compensation and panel vendor must be set by the research team.
extensions.label: Generalizability

extensions.title: No debate visible in the retrieved works
extensions.why: The retrieved literature (COVID, AI, media education) does not bear directly on sharing from ties, so I decline to invent a debate. Instead this brief tests the measurement cause: whether sharing and plausibility are distinct.
extensions.rationale: The source study found that plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely (both showed the same misinformation penalty), but it measured them in the same conjoint task with no manipulation that could dissociate them. This follow-up tests whether sharing and plausibility are separable constructs by introducing an accuracy-salience prompt that should reduce sharing of misinformation without changing perceived plausibility, and by measuring the two outcomes in counterbalanced blocks to rule out order confounds.
extensions.contribution: Establishes whether the sharing–plausibility correlation observed in the source conjoint reflects a single underlying judgment or two separable processes, with direct implications for how to model and intervene on misinformation sharing.
extensions.hypothesis: The accuracy-salience prompt will narrow the misinformation sharing gap (false vs true/neutral) by at least 0.031 standard units relative to the control arm, while leaving the plausibility gap unchanged, demonstrating that sharing and plausibility are separable processes.
extensions.primary_outcome: Primary outcome: sharing intention, measured as a binary share/don't-share choice for each headline profile (same as source study). Secondary outcome: plausibility, measured on a 0–100 slider ('How plausible is this claim?') for the same profiles. The key estimand is the interaction between accuracy prompt and information type (false vs true/neutral) on sharing, tested against the null that the prompt does not differentially reduce sharing of false headlines. A secondary estimand is the same interaction on plausibility, expected to be null if the constructs are separable.
extensions.comparison: Accuracy-salience prompt (binary, between-respondent randomization): in the prompt arm, before each sharing decision the respondent sees the instruction 'Before you decide, consider whether this claim is accurate.' In the control arm, no such instruction appears. The prompt is the manipulated variable; its variation comes from random assignment at the respondent level. Within each arm, the order in which plausibility and sharing blocks appear is counterbalanced (plausibility-first vs sharing-first, randomized per respondent) to separate the two outcome measures from order effects.
unresolved: Demand characteristics: respondents who notice the accuracy prompt may share less across all content, not just misinformation, confounding the interaction. Mitigated by including true/neutral and fact-check headlines as within-respondent controls.

Construct drift: the prompt may shift the meaning of 'plausible' (e.g., respondents start equating plausibility with accuracy), producing a spurious null on plausibility. Mitigated by a post-hoc probe asking respondents to define 'plausible' in their own words (qualitative, not in primary analysis).

Order effects: if plausibility is rated first, it may anchor the sharing decision (or vice versa). Mitigated by the counterbalanced block design and a pre-specified equivalence test on the order × information-type interaction.

Panel fatigue and attrition: a within-subject design with multiple profiles per respondent may produce fatigue, inflating noise. Mitigated by capping the number of profiles per respondent and monitoring completion rates.

The prompt may be too weak to move sharing at all, producing a null that is uninformative about separability. Mitigated by the power calculation targeting a 0.031 effect and by a pre-specified dose-response check (if available, a two-level prompt: mild vs strong accuracy reminder).

data_sources: YouGov US panel (same platform as source study): provides the respondent sample, demographic and attitudinal covariates, and the delivery infrastructure for the online experiment.

Source-study headline pool (12 headlines: 4 true/neutral, 4 false, 4 fact-check, as used in the registered conjoint): provides the stimulus set, ensuring comparability of the misinformation penalty estimate with the source study's −18.2-point finding.

Pre-registered analysis code and stimulus materials from the source study's OSF repository: provides the exact headline texts, fact-check texts, and conjoint profile structure for replication of the stimulus set.
plan.units: Individual US adult panel respondents (N ≈ 3,200 total; ~1,600 per accuracy-salience arm). Each respondent completes the full within-subject design, so the unit of analysis for the primary contrast is the respondent, with headline-level observations nested within respondents.
plan.exposure: Accuracy-salience prompt (binary, between-respondent randomization): in the prompt arm, before each sharing decision the respondent sees the instruction 'Before you decide, consider whether this claim is accurate.' In the control arm, no such instruction appears. The prompt is the manipulated variable; its variation comes from random assignment at the respondent level. Within each arm, the order in which plausibility and sharing blocks appear is counterbalanced (plausibility-first vs sharing-first, randomized per respondent) to separate the two outcome measures from order effects.
plan.outcome: Primary outcome: sharing intention, measured as a binary share/don't-share choice for each headline profile (same as source study). Secondary outcome: plausibility, measured on a 0–100 slider ('How plausible is this claim?') for the same profiles. The key estimand is the interaction between accuracy prompt and information type (false vs true/neutral) on sharing, tested against the null that the prompt does not differentially reduce sharing of false headlines. A secondary estimand is the same interaction on plausibility, expected to be null if the constructs are separable.
plan.identification: Two comparisons do the work. First, within the prompt arm, compare the sharing gap (false minus true/neutral) to the sharing gap in the control arm: if the prompt selectively narrows the misinformation gap on sharing while leaving the plausibility gap unchanged, sharing and plausibility are separable. Second, the counterbalanced block order (plausibility-first vs sharing-first) is used to verify that the sharing–plausibility correlation is not an artifact of measuring one immediately after the other. What must hold: the prompt must not change perceived plausibility (verified by the null interaction on plausibility), and the two block orders must produce equivalent estimates (verified by a pre-specified equivalence test).
threats: Demand characteristics: respondents who notice the accuracy prompt may share less across all content, not just misinformation, confounding the interaction. Mitigated by including true/neutral and fact-check headlines as within-respondent controls.

Construct drift: the prompt may shift the meaning of 'plausible' (e.g., respondents start equating plausibility with accuracy), producing a spurious null on plausibility. Mitigated by a post-hoc probe asking respondents to define 'plausible' in their own words (qualitative, not in primary analysis).

Order effects: if plausibility is rated first, it may anchor the sharing decision (or vice versa). Mitigated by the counterbalanced block design and a pre-specified equivalence test on the order × information-type interaction.

Panel fatigue and attrition: a within-subject design with multiple profiles per respondent may produce fatigue, inflating noise. Mitigated by capping the number of profiles per respondent and monitoring completion rates.

The prompt may be too weak to move sharing at all, producing a null that is uninformative about separability. Mitigated by the power calculation targeting a 0.031 effect and by a pre-specified dose-response check (if available, a two-level prompt: mild vs strong accuracy reminder).
plan.analysis_plan: Estimator: linear mixed model with random intercepts for respondents and random slopes for information type, fitted separately for sharing (binary, logit link) and plausibility (continuous, identity link). Adjustment set: respondent age, sex, education, political ideology (same covariates as source study), block order (plausibility-first vs sharing-first), and wave (if multi-wave). Standard errors: cluster-robust at the respondent level (accounting for within-respondent correlation across profiles). Pre-specified tests: (1) Interaction of accuracy prompt × information type (false vs true/neutral) on sharing — primary test, two-sided α = 0.05, with a pre-registered equivalence margin of ±0.015 to distinguish 'no effect' from 'underpowered null.' (2) Same interaction on plausibility — secondary test, same α and equivalence margin. (3) Equivalence test on block order × information type interaction (TOST, equivalence margin ±0.01) to confirm order does not confound the sharing–plausibility relationship. Power: with ~1,600 respondents per arm and ~12 profiles per respondent, the design is powered to detect a 0.031 difference in the misinformation sharing gap between prompt and control arms at 80% power, α = 0.05, assuming a within-respondent correlation of 0.30 across profiles (conservative relative to the source study's observed ICC).

extensions.label: Theoretical debate

takeaways: In this registered conjoint, information type shaped sharing most: misinformation headlines were chosen 18.2 points less often than true/neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001).
Fact-check headlines were also chosen less often than true/neutral ones, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility ratings tracked sharing closely.

Among measured sharer attributes, close ties raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]); origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero.
Registered subgroups showed that respondents with higher belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with lower belief (p < 0.001), and true/neutral content less.
Many tests were run without correction, sharer attributes are measured rather than randomized, and the ideology and subgroup findings sit near conventional thresholds.
sections_draft.abstract: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Plausibility showed a similar pattern. Among the measured source attributes, close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) raised sharing, while origin, knowledge and conspiracy belief were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation more. Caveats: many uncorrected tests, and the source attributes are measured, not randomized.
sections_draft.design_notes: Respondents were a YouGov sample of US adults, and the analysis used all 12,000 raw profile ratings, with none dropped for missing values on the main outcomes. Each profile attributed a headline to one of the respondent's real contacts. Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact were randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are measured attributes of those contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes, not causal effects. True/neutral headlines are the reference level for information type (3,854 misinformation and 3,972 fact-check profiles were eligible). Standard errors are clustered by respondent, and tests are two-sided.

results.H1: Information type had large effects on sharing. Misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p < 0.001). Chosen shares were 60.3% for true/neutral, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. These are causal contrasts, because headline type was randomized.
results.H2: Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p = 0.003). This is a descriptive contrast on a measured attribute.
results.H3: Continental US origin was 0.2 points above foreign origin (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p = 0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero.
results.H4: A moderate sharer was chosen 1.9 points less often than a liberal sharer (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p = 0.034), a small difference close to the threshold. Conservative sharers were not distinguishable from liberal ones (−0.7 points, 95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]).
results.H5: High trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points over low trust (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p < 0.001). Mid trust was 3.6 points higher, with an interval that includes zero (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]).
results.H6: Neither mid nor high sharer knowledge was distinguishable from low. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]); mid was about zero.
results.H7: A sharer with high belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from one with low belief on sharing (−0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p = 0.87).
results.H8: Misinformation was rated more plausible 18.6 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p < 0.001), and fact-checks 12.4 points less often (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p < 0.001). The pattern closely mirrors sharing.
results.H9: Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points over distant ties (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p = 0.008), a modest effect on a measured attribute.
results.H10: Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.3 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.4]).
results.H11: Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal ones (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p = 0.026), a small effect near the threshold. Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.H12: Neither mid nor high trust was distinguishable from low for plausibility. High trust was 2.5 points higher (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]).
results.H13: Sharer knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High knowledge was 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]); mid was about zero.
results.H14: Sharer belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (0.0 points, 95% CI [−1.8, 1.8]).
results.RW: Re-weighting each source attribute by the inverse of its assignment probability left the picture largely unchanged. Close ties still raised sharing by 3.0 points and plausibility by 2.7 points, and high trust raised sharing by 6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The moderate-sharer effect on sharing weakened to −1.7 points (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0]), while its effect on plausibility stayed at −2.1 points. High trust on plausibility remained not distinguishable from zero. The other estimates were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S1: Age moderated the response to information type. Respondents in the highest age tertile shared misinformation 6.1 points less than the lowest tertile (p < 0.001). Differences for the other levels were not distinguishable from zero. These are descriptive subgroup contrasts.
results.S2: Respondent ideology mattered for a few levels. More conservative respondents shared true/neutral headlines 5.6 points less (p = 0.002), shared less from continental US sharers (−1.6 points, p = 0.005), and shared less from liberal sharers (−4.8 points, p = 0.017). Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S3: Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with the least (p < 0.001) and true/neutral headlines 5.5 points less (p < 0.001). They also shared less from high-trust sharers (−2.3 points, p < 0.001) and continental US sharers (−1.7 points, p = 0.002).
results.S4: Respondents with higher media trust shared misinformation 4.8 points more than those with low media trust (p = 0.003). They also shared less from high-knowledge sharers (−2.4 points, p = 0.028) and more from low-conspiracy sharers (+3.5 points, p = 0.032). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S5: Spanish-language respondents shared misinformation 3.6 points more than English-language ones (p = 0.010). They also shared more from low-trust sharers (+7.9 points, p = 0.022) and low-knowledge sharers (+3.2 points, p = 0.038). Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero, and with many comparisons some of these may be chance.
results.S6: Older respondents rated misinformation 4.0 points less plausible than younger ones (p = 0.013), and liberal sharers 3.7 points more plausible (p = 0.020). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S7: More conservative respondents rated true/neutral headlines 4.9 points less plausible (p = 0.006) and continental-US-attributed profiles 1.5 points less plausible (p = 0.009). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S8: Respondents with greater belief in disputed claims rated misinformation 6.8 points more plausible (p < 0.001) and true/neutral headlines 6.9 points less plausible (p < 0.001). They also gave lower plausibility to high-trust sharers (−2.4 points, p < 0.001) and high-knowledge sharers (−3.6 points, p = 0.002).
results.S9: Respondents with higher media trust rated misinformation 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-conspiracy sharers 4.4 points more plausible (p = 0.009). They rated high-knowledge sharers 2.6 points less plausible (p = 0.019).
results.S10: Spanish-language respondents rated misinformation 3.7 points more plausible than English-language ones (p = 0.008). They also rated low-trust sharers 9.0 points more plausible (p = 0.007) and low-knowledge sharers 3.6 points more plausible (p = 0.016). These are post hoc-looking subgroup contrasts among many tests.
results.X1: This is a post hoc analysis. Each extra point of trust in the sharer (on the 1–5 scale) was associated with 1.4 points more sharing (p < 0.001, two-sided).
results.X2: This is a post hoc analysis. Each extra point of trust was associated with 1.3 points higher plausibility (p < 0.001, two-sided).
results.X3: This is a post hoc analysis. The close-tie premium on sharing was 2.9 points (p = 0.006, two-sided), consistent with the registered estimate.
results.X4: Post hoc. Among profiles chosen for sharing, misinformation was 5.5 points more likely than true/neutral to be one the respondent judged less plausible than the other post (95% CI [3.0, 8.1], p < 0.001). Fact-checks were 1.7 points higher (95% CI [−0.5, 4.0]).
results.X5: Post hoc. Sharing was 4.4 points higher when respondent and sharer leaned the same way than when they leaned opposite (95% CI [0.9, 7.9], p = 0.015). Pairs involving a moderate were not distinguishable from opposite leans (0.8 points).
results.X6: Post hoc. Among misinformation profiles, a higher network mean perceived belief in disputed claims was associated with more sharing (coefficient 0.110, p = 0.026, n = 3,196). This is a modest association, near the threshold.
results.X7: Post hoc. Among partisan respondents, congenial slanted headlines were shared 2.5 points more than uncongenial ones, not distinguishable from zero (p = 0.18, n = 3,016).
results.X8: Post hoc. The slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero overall (0.005, p = 0.71).
results.X9: Post hoc. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero overall (−0.005, p = 0.72).
results.X10: Post hoc and thin (n = 266). The anti-vaccine misinformation headline was rated 16.5 points more plausible when the sharer was seen as believing the DNA claim (p = 0.013). Treat with caution.
results.X11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 1.9 points per trust point across headlines (p = 0.013), a small association.
results.X12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on sharing misinformation was 3.5 points (p = 0.040), near the threshold.
results.X13: Post hoc. Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero in the pooled slope (0.002, p = 0.78), matching H3.
results.XS1: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing was 1.7 points for fact-checks, 1.9 for misinformation and 0.6 for true/neutral headlines. The differences between slopes were not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS2: Post hoc. The trust slope on plausibility was about 1.8 points for fact-checks and 2.1 for misinformation, and about zero for true/neutral headlines. Differences between slopes were not clearly distinguishable.
results.XS3: Post hoc. The close-tie premium was 4.7 points for fact-checks, 3.5 for misinformation and 0.9 for true/neutral headlines. The gap between true/neutral and fact-checks was borderline (p = 0.050).
results.XS5: Post hoc. The congruent-versus-opposite sharing gap was between 3.8 and 5.6 points within each information type, with intervals including zero. The differences between types were not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS7: Post hoc. Congenial misinformation was shared 5.4 points more than uncongenial misinformation (p = 0.012), but there was no such gap for fact-checks (−0.2 points). The difference between the two was 5.6 points (p = 0.007).
results.XS8: Post hoc. For misinformation, sharing rose with the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (slope 0.086, p = 0.002), while slopes for fact-checks and true/neutral headlines were not distinguishable from zero. The difference from fact-checks was 0.131 (p = 0.001).
results.XS9: Post hoc. Plausibility of misinformation rose with the sharer's perceived conspiracy belief (slope 0.095, p < 0.001), but fell slightly for true/neutral headlines (−0.055, p = 0.046). The difference from fact-checks was 0.146 for misinformation (p < 0.001).
results.XS11: Post hoc. The trust slope on sharing misinformation was 2.5 points for health and 1.9 for political headlines. The difference was not distinguishable from zero, and the health group was small (n = 550).
results.XS12: Post hoc. The close-tie premium on misinformation was 0.7 points for health and 3.9 for political headlines. The difference was not distinguishable from zero, and the health group was small.
results.XS13a: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was near zero in both English (0.004) and Spanish (0.000), and the difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS13b: Post hoc. The sharer-origin slope was 1.3 points among foreign-born and −0.8 points among US-born respondents. Neither was distinguishable from zero, nor was the difference.

sections_draft.limitations: Many tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so the smaller effects (moderate sharer, close tie on plausibility, several subgroup contrasts) may be chance findings. Only headline type was randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and conspiracy belief are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so those AMCEs bundle correlated attributes and are not causal. Non-significant results are inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Health-topic and other subgroups are small. The exploratory X and XS analyses were specified after seeing the data and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

got_right: Randomized information type with a registered plan produced a clean causal result: misinformation −18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks −13.3 points on sharing, against a 0.031 MDE.

Source attributes (tie, trust, ideology, knowledge) were taken from respondents' real contacts, which gives an ego-network setting. The report labels them honestly as measured associations, not causal effects.

The inverse-probability re-weighting (R1–R12) left the estimates essentially unchanged: close tie 0.030, high trust 0.067. The weighted moderate-sharer contrast was correctly flagged as non-significant (p = 0.056).

Sharing and plausibility were measured for every profile and gave near-identical patterns (H1 vs H8). The registered subgroup on belief in disputed claims (S3, S8) shows a coherent respondent-level moderation.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The 'who' and 'from whom' questions in the title rest on contact attributes that were not randomized, so tie, trust, ideology and the rest bundle with the real person. The only causal result is the headline-type effect, which is expected and well known.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Only infotype is randomized; H2 and H5 are descriptive contrasts (close tie +0.030, high trust +0.057).

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The trust and knowledge contrasts compare against thin reference cells, and the MDEs are optimistic because they ignore clustering. Null findings there are therefore inconclusive.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Trust: low n=828, MDE 0.051–0.056 vs observed mid 0.036; Knowledge: low n=2065, MDE 0.037 vs observed high 0.017.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Many uncorrected tests (14 hypotheses, 12 re-weighted, about 10 subgroup tables with 18 rows each). Several subgroup findings sit near the threshold and are likely chance.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: S5 low-trust cell +7.9 points, p=0.022, with 257 and 571 profiles; H4 moderate sharer p=0.034.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Sharing was a forced choice between two profiles, and the study offers no behavioural outcome or check on real-world sharing. Plausibility mirrors sharing so closely that the two outcomes may not be distinct constructs.

The belief-in-disputed-claims subgroup effect on misinformation sharing (+5.6 points) is the most interesting result, but it is a registered subgroup contrast, not a manipulated mechanism, so the study cannot say why.

briefs.title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
briefs.question: Does a sharer's tie strength or trust causally change willingness to share a false headline?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the design cause: randomizing attributes in vignettes turns the descriptive close-tie and high-trust contrasts into causal estimates and removes bundling with the real contact.
briefs.design_sketch: Crossed vignette: headline type (true, false, fact-check) x randomized sharer tie (close/distant) x randomized trust (high/low) shown as a forwarded post. The outcome is a real share to a mock feed, plus plausibility. Include a within-respondent block with each respondent's real contact as a benchmark. Sample is a YouGov-type US panel, with respondent clustering handled in the analysis.

power_target.basis: H2 close tie 0.030 vs MDE 0.0258; H5 high trust 0.057 vs MDE 0.051

briefs.title: No debate visible in the retrieved works
briefs.question: Not applicable: the retrieved works do not frame a live disagreement that this design can discriminate.
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: The retrieved literature (COVID, AI, media education) does not bear directly on sharing from ties, so I decline to invent a debate. Instead this brief tests the measurement cause: whether sharing and plausibility are distinct.
briefs.design_sketch: Within-respondent design that measures plausibility, then sharing, in separate counterbalanced blocks, and adds a manipulation of accuracy salience (accuracy prompt vs none). If the misinformation sharing gap closes under the prompt while plausibility stays fixed, the two are separable. Use the same headline pool and a US panel.

power_target.basis: H1 MDE 0.031; observed misinformation effect −0.182 leaves ample margin for detecting a partial reduction

briefs.title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
briefs.question: Is the gap in sharing misinformation vs true content smaller among respondents high in belief in disputed claims, and does the pattern hold in Spanish-language samples?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the missing_moderator cause: it pre-selects the moderator from S3 and S8 and tests it with enough power instead of relying on a tertile contrast.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomize headline type, stratifying recruitment by belief-in-disputed-claims tertile and by survey language (English/Spanish). Use the same share and plausibility outcomes. Estimate the infotype x moderator interaction with respondent-clustered SEs. Pre-register a single primary interaction.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: respondent belief in disputed claims (tertile) and survey language

power_target.basis: S3 misinformation difference 0.056 (SE 0.017); interaction MDE is larger than main-effect MDE 0.031

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but the headline-type effect is already settled and adds nothing new. The retrieved literature shows no genuine debate this study bears on, so the debate brief is replaced by a measurement test. Run the advance_design brief first: randomizing tie and trust with a behavioural share is the only way to turn the study's most interesting claims (close ties and high trust) into causal estimates. The moderator brief should follow, sized to the 0.056 subgroup gap.
